Elon Musk has an interesting theory about dating intelligence agents 😂

Back in 2025, Musk shared a joke he overheard at a party:

“If your girlfriend is a 10, she’s an asset.”

And no, he wasn’t talking about her being a valuable partner. In intelligence circles, an “asset” can mean a recruited informant or intelligence source.

Musk then added the punchline: “What I meant was: if your girlfriend is a 10, YOU are the valuable asset.”

💻 Describe a map app in plain words and Gemini builds it, with real Google Maps inside

Google AI Studio can now plug Google Maps straight into the apps Gemini writes. You type something like "Build an interactive 3D tour of NYC showcasing iconic landmarks", and a live, working map loads in the preview.

The apps can use real map data: 3D buildings, Street View, places, routes, weather and air quality. Google's own examples include a store finder, a road-trip planner and a route planner for a mobile pet-grooming business.

Setup takes one click and no credit card. Free use is capped at 100 calls a day for each Maps API. Launching a real app means linking a paid Google Cloud account.

💻 Obsidian's CEO and Cloudflare put their AI coding setups on GitHub for free

All five are free skill packs that work in Claude Code and Codex. The most popular one comes from a TypeScript teacher.

1. Matt Pocock's skills (319K stars). His everyday kit: tests first, a spec before code, and a code review run by two separate agents.

2. Addy Osmani's agent skills (114K), from an engineer on Anthropic's Claude Code team. One command for each step, from /spec to /ship.

3. Cloudflare's security audit (67K). Agents hunt for vulnerabilities, then a fresh agent tries to disprove each one.

4. Obsidian skills (51K) by CEO Steph Ango. Your agent writes proper Obsidian notes, Bases and canvases.

5. Elephant-Goldfish (16K), on Google's GitHub. One AI drafts the design. Fresh AIs that never saw the chat review it.

Google's repo notes it is not an officially supported Google product.

🤖 Claude got an empty folder and built an operating system in eight days

An Anthropic engineer gave the new Claude Fable 5.2 an empty folder and asked for a prototype operating system. The model coordinated more than 1,000 subagents that wrote, tested and reviewed code around the clock for eight days.

The result boots on a laptop. It has its own core, drivers for the disk, keyboard and network, file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer and Claude built in.

Anthropic shared the test as it released Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 on Monday. A team of 1,000 Fable agents also turned the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem into a form a computer can check, in 30 hours. Anthropic's first attempt, with a human guiding it, took 11 days.

Fable 5.2 is open to all users. Mythos 5.2, the same model with fewer cyber and biology safeguards, is only for vetted organizations.

Anthropic says Claude now writes over 90% of the changes merged into its core codebase, with human guidance.

😳 WTF. THIS AI PERSONA REACTS WHILE YOU'RE STILL TALKING

Meet Emma from Nuance Labs, with a face and voice licensed from a real actress. Its reply timing overlapped a real speaker 89% of the time, versus 35% for the next best.

Most AI personas stare blankly while you talk. Emma reacts while you’re still speaking.

AI is coming 🐺

❗️Microsoft wants AI to rewrite reality and make it look like you said it

Imagine watching a live interview where someone says something controversial. But instead of hearing their actual words, AI replaces them with something completely different. Their lips move in perfect sync, making it look like they said it all along.

That’s the idea behind a new Microsoft patent describing technology that could alter speech and lip movements in real time.

The system would analyze a person’s voice and video, identify words that need changing, and use generative AI to replace them while adjusting their mouth movements to match. The result could look like an entirely natural recording, even though the original speech has been altered.

Microsoft’s proposed applications go far beyond simple video editing. The technology could translate someone’s speech into another language while making their lips match the translation, remove profanity, correct mispronunciations and even eliminate filler words like “um”. It could also potentially rewrite statements using information gathered from online sources or generate shorter videos where people appear to deliver AI-written summaries.

But there’s one particularly unsettling possibility: two people watching the same live broadcast could hear and see completely different versions of what was said, depending on their individual preferences.

Think about that for a moment. You could watch an interview, discuss it with a friend, and discover that you both saw different versions of the exact same conversation.

The technology could make translation and video editing much more powerful, but it also raises serious questions about censorship, misinformation and the future of trust in video evidence.
